1.1: 1.1 Preface. Solomon, son of David, king of Israel, produced three volumes according to the number of his names. The first of these is Mishle, which the Greeks and Latins call Proverbs, because in it, under comparative likeness, he shows figures of words and images of the truth, but reserved the truth itself to be understood by the ingenuity of the readers. The second book he called Coheleth, which is called in Greek and in Latin Concionator (the Preacher), because its addresses are directed not only spiritually to one person, as in Proverbs, but to all generally, teaching that all things we see in the world are vain and brief, and for that reason by no means to be sought. The third book he entitled Shir Hashirim, which is turned into the Latin tongue as Song of Songs, where through a wedding song he sings mystically of the union of Christ and the Church. It is called the Song of Songs because it is preferred to all songs, just as in the law certain things are called holy, above which are greater, the holy of holies. In these three books he composed the disciplines of three kinds, by which knowledge of things is reached: first ethics, that is, moral; after this physics, which comprehends the quality of nature; finally theoretics, that is, contemplative. For in Proverbs, teaching moral matters, through a certain common usage of speech he put forth a loftier understanding, and in concise words and brief sentences he fits together the keeping of the commandments and the instruction of heavenly teaching. Proverbs are those which explain one thing under other words, which are understood otherwise than as they are said; they have more in the force of their meanings than in the sound of their words; the Greeks call them [a Greek term omitted]. Ecclesiastes, examining the natures of things, finds all things in the world to be vain and perishing, and, having observed the fragility of all things, warned men to renounce the world. In the Song of Songs, rising above visible things and contemplating those that are heavenly or divine, under the appearance of bridegroom and bride he declares the unity of Christ and the Church, and, stirring the soul to the love of heavenly things, summons it to come to fellowship with God. But one must not think what is handed down by our hearers, that among the Hebrews this was the practice, that they would permit no one to read this book unless a man already of perfect knowledge and of strengthened faith in skill, lest the knowledge instruct slippery minds less than the text turn them to bodily desires. Solomon, that is, peaceable, because in his reign there was peace, by which the future peace of the Church was prefigured; Jedidiah, that is, beloved, and it signifies him of whom it is said: You are beautiful in form above the sons of men; therefore God has blessed you forever (Psalm 44). Ecclesiastes, that is, preacher, and it signifies him who was to speak reasonably and to gather the Church. According to the number of his names, he made three books: Proverbs, in which he teaches little ones, not so much in age as in wisdom, about calm conduct in the world, namely how they may lawfully use temporal things; Ecclesiastes, in which he instructs men of more advanced age to despise perishable things; the Song of Songs, namely this work, in which he teaches the perfected man about the love of God alone, that he may rest between the arms of the bridegroom. Hence it is also called the Song of Songs, excelling all other songs in its dignity. For through those vices are avoided and the enemy guarded against; through these we are enriched with virtues and joined to the Lord. In a similar order the philosophers also set out their teachings: first they teach ethics, afterward physics, and one whom they see to have advanced in these they lead on up to theoretics. The subject matter: the bridegroom and the bride, that is, the head and the Church. And the manner: with what desire the members cling to the head and strive to please him, and what gifts they receive from him either in the present or look for in the future, and with what affection the bridegroom loves the Church, praising her, and admonishing, and strengthening her. The end is the love of God. In this work I seem to myself to find four persons: the bridegroom and his companions, the bride and the maidens with her. Some things are said by the bridegroom, some by the bride; a number by the young women, certain ones by the companions of the bridegroom. It is fitting indeed that at the beginning there be a multitude of maidens with the bride, a crowd of young men with the bridegroom. By the bridegroom understand Christ; by the bride the Church without spot or wrinkle. By the friends of the bridegroom understand the angels, and those who have attained to the perfect man. The maidens are the crowds of beginning brides, who have obtained salvation in a certain measure. From this book the Gentiles claimed for themselves the wedding song, and a song of this kind was adopted. If you wish to ascend to the Song of Songs, it is necessary to go out of Egypt, so that after the crossing of the Red Sea, with the enemies drowned, you may first be able to sing the song: Let us sing to the Lord, for he is gloriously, etc. (Exodus 15). But since you are still far from the Song of Songs, travel spiritually through the land of the desert, and then, set at the bank of the Jordan, sing the second song: Hear, O heavens, the things I speak, etc. (Deuteronomy 31). And when you have passed over all, ascend to higher things, so that as a soul adorned with the bridegroom you may sing this Song of Songs also. It is to be noted that the bride always desires to stay in the house, or in the bed, or in some inner place with the bridegroom, which suits women. He, as is the way of males, summons his beloved to the outer parts of the vineyards, or to works of this kind, because the Church, if it could be, desires to raise offspring for the Lord in the tranquility of peace. But he in the present exercises her with frequent persecutions, that she may come the purer to eternal things, lest, if prosperity befall her, delighted by sojourning in the present age or exile, she sigh less for the heavenly homeland. The Synagogue is a congregation, which is said also of stones; the Church is a convocation, which is said of rational beings. But each portion of the just, in the same faith and love of Christ at different times, the one by awaiting him who was to come, the other by receiving him who is present, has been made a sharer. God, the founder of the universe, created all the motions of the soul for good, but through our use it often happens that things which are good by nature, while we abuse them badly, lead us to sin. One of the motions of the soul is love, which we use well if we love wisdom and truth, but badly if we love flesh or blood. You, therefore, as a spiritual person, hear spiritually the loving words of the song being sung, and learn to transfer the motion of your soul and the fire of natural love to better things. Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. The voice of those who precede the coming of Christ, who pray to the father of the bridegroom, that is, of Christ. In the midst of their prayers she is heard, and seeing the bridegroom she speaks to him: Let him touch me with the sweetness of his presence, which I have heard oftentimes promised by the prophets, and, bringing as it were a kiss, let him also receive the touch of my mouth; that is, let him hear me as I ask about the way of salvation, and, making both one, let him bring the kiss of peace. To kiss is put for to be reconciled, after the likeness of those who withdrew from their lords on account of discord, but, returning, kiss one another and are perfectly reconciled; so the Synagogue, the human race removed from God by sin, wishes to be reconciled through the incarnation of the Son. As many commandments as she learns from his preaching, so many kisses of his mouth she receives, as it were. She speaks in the manner of a lover, who in the fervor of love cannot keep the order of speaking. For as in a kiss two different bodies are joined, so in the incarnation of the Son two substances, of divinity and humanity, utterly different, are united in an inseparable union. For your breasts are better. She names the breasts of the bridegroom Christ, which is a womanly thing, to show from the very beginning of the song that she speaks figuratively. Therefore I desire the kiss, which is also my redemption, because your instructions, which are the milk and nourishment of children, are better than other teachings, which do not cherish but kill the simple, as wine kills little ones. By the fragrance of ointments the reputation of virtues is usually signified.
1.2: 1.2 Your name is oil poured out. Therefore I also desire the kiss, because your name is oil, etc. The bridegroom came from the Father to the bride anointed, that he might also anoint the bride. Christ is from chrisma, that is, anointed from anointing; which name is poured out through the grace of the Holy Spirit in baptism upon all the faithful. I cannot yet embrace you yourself; in the meantime your name, out of longing for you, will spend the night with me. The name of Jesus came into the world, and at once is preached. Oil poured out, that is, over the whole earth the name of Christ is preached; now the name of Moses is heard among the Gentiles, which before was confined only in the narrow bounds of Judea. Therefore the maidens have loved you. Saying this, she catches sight of the maidens, who were not present while she was speaking before, but in the midst of the prayers the chorus of maidens enters and is praised in the words of the bride. All the Churches, which make up the one catholic Church, are the maidens: not aged by guilt but new by grace, not barren with old age but, by the age of the mind, suited for spiritual fruitfulness. And because with the oil of your grace you have emptied out all the sorrows of crimes, Therefore the maidens, etc.
1.3: 1.3 Draw me after you. The maidens answer: Draw me after you. The bride does not follow behind the back, but, joined to the bridegroom's side, her handmaids go in after her. Draw me after you. Up to this point is the voice of those awaiting the incarnation of the Savior and commending his gifts; from here follows the voice of those who came to the faith after the time of the incarnation. The former asked that he come and offer a kiss; the latter do not so demand that he descend to them, but desire rather to follow him themselves to the heavens; and because she sees this cannot be done by herself, she implores the guidance of him to whom she desires to come. Unto the fragrance of your ointments. In the consideration of the miracles. The king has brought me in, etc. The bride, having entered the inner chamber of the bridegroom, returns to the young women and announces to them: He has brought me in. Or, through hope he has led me into eternal blessedness; in the plural, for the fullness of every kind of good, as if I had already tasted beforehand the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom; the things prepared for me in heaven I have come to know by his own revealing; and soon, turned to him who reveals this to her, she gives thanks for the benefits. There are four things in a house: the gate, the ascent, the dining hall, the bedchamber. By the gate we understand faith; by the ascent, hope; by the dining hall, charity; by the bedchamber, blessedness itself. We will exult and rejoice. As if she said: We do not exalt ourselves over the gifts received, but exalt you, mindful in all things with what great kindness you deigned to soften the austerity of the law by the grace of the gospel faith; therefore we will exult not in ourselves but in you, because all the upright love you, and have learned that you are to be loved above all things. Again the bride has entered the inner chamber, and the maidens, while they await her coming, sing joyfully together for the perfection of the bride. Mindful of your breasts. And the upright love: this is referred to the commendation of the bride. Mindful of your breasts, etc. She who is greater already enjoys the milk of your breasts. We too do not indeed love, but we shall love. Then they speak to the bridegroom: The upright love you. The upright: all who are upright of heart love you above all things, and they are not upright who put anything before your love, from whom alone they have whatever good they have. The upright love. In vain do they believe they love the Creator who despise his admonitions. The truly just violate God neither in deed, nor in thought, nor in word.
1.4: 1.4 I am black. After the Church was led into the cellars, that is, through knowledge and through hope of the good things to come, after she learned to love him with an upright heart and to rejoice in his grace, it remains to show that for love of him and for the acquisition of the goods she has tasted she undergoes the struggle, and what affliction she bears. I am black. As if she said: You promise that you will go with me, and the tribulation which I suffer can deter you; but let neither affliction nor ill repute deter you, because these will confer the beauty of the virtues, and after love there remains patience for the proof of love. I am black. Again the bride answers the maidens, and the matter treated is manifest temptation. I am black. I appear indeed contemptible in the eyes of the persecutors, but before God I shine glorious by the confession of the truth. Like the tents of Kedar. Here like is put not for the truth but for the estimation of the foolish, who think her the dwelling of vices or of demons; like the skins of Solomon is put here for the truth. Kedar was a son of Ishmael, whose hand was against all, and the hand of all against him, having no place among men, but dwelling always in tents, because of wickedness and wrath. So the just also are believed, on account of their merits, to be driven out and afflicted, and are judged as enemies of all; hence it is said: You shall be hated by all men for my name's sake (Matthew 10). Like the feet. The Church, mortifying carnal desires in herself and adorned with virtues, becomes a worthy dwelling for the true Peaceable One. Therefore the flesh of the Lord's humanity is called a skin, because as a tent is stretched over someone lest he be scorched by the sun, so the flesh of Christ stretched on the cross was for us a shading from vices.
1.5: 1.5 The sun has discolored me. It belongs to the sun to burn and to illuminate; so the true sun outwardly burns his own with persecutions, and by giving strength to resist, enlightens them. The sons of my mother. And, as if to the objection of the weak who doubt, she answers: She shows whence she bore the first fury of the persecutors, which appears the more grievous in that it comes from fellow-sufferers. The sons, that is, the apostles, destroyed our sect. Paul, persecutor of the Church, was a son of her mother according to the flesh and upbringing; and doing penance, turned to the signs of the sister, he preached the faith which he formerly destroyed. They have made me. There was one vineyard of Christ in Jerusalem, namely the primitive Church, which was established on the day of Pentecost by the coming of the Holy Spirit, and of which the apostles were at that time the keepers; but when persecution arose they were scattered in the regions of Judea and Samaria, except the apostles, and so it happened that there were many vineyards, that is, in many places. And while the Jewish persecutors wished to disturb the Church, they spread the seedbed of the word more widely, unwilling, and by persecuting one, caused many to be established. Having then said that she was afflicted by the parricidal hatred of the Synagogue, she soon adds how much she has gained by this affliction, adding in the person of those to whom the care of preaching was committed: They have made me keeper in the vineyards. GREGORY. Our vineyards are our actions, which we cultivate by the practice of daily labor. But set as keepers in the vineyards, we do not keep our own vineyard, because while we are entangled in external actions, we neglect the ministry of our own action. While I was keeping many vineyards, in order to gain others, in some I sustained losses. The bitterness of the persecution by the sons of the Synagogue made me not keep my own vineyard, because, the gospel teaching having been abandoned, they were forcing me to the differences of legal observances.
1.6: 1.6 Show me, etc. The voice of the Church beginning from the Gentiles to the bride, because many false prophets go out into the world saying: Behold, here is Christ, behold, there; she begs that she may be able to discern in whose profession and work he can be found. Show me my shepherd, whom my whole soul loves, and in whom he has rest and pastures, lest, disturbed by the heat of temptations, I begin to seek him through the gatherings of companions, that is, of heretics. Or it is in the voice of the preachers to the bridegroom, that they may be able to discern to whom they ought to minister the words of life. Then she beholds the bridegroom, who, once beheld, departed. And this he does frequently in the whole song, which she has proved by experience in herself: the bridegroom, often held, often slips away, until he is truly held. At noon, etc. That is, in the splendor of your majesty, which befits the perfect, not at morning or evening. Or, at noon, that is, in the burning of tribulations, which the devil sends, grieving that the world is being snatched from him. The quality of things is usually noted from the time. Abraham received the angels at noon. Joseph feasts with his brothers at noon. Of your companions. Heretics are called companions, because they carry about the mysteries of his name and confession.
1.7: 1.7 If you do not know. Because the bride, while seeking the aid of God's presence in tribulations, had added, in the person of the weak, Lest I begin to wander, the bridegroom, being implored, at once rebukes that same trembling with kindly reproach, according to the Gospel saying, O you of little faith (Matthew 14), as if he said: You fear being destroyed by me in tribulation, and in the heat you complain that you have been blackened; but I have determined by tribulations to make you more beautiful. But if perhaps you do not know this, nor remember that no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully, go out from my company. GREGORY, Moralia, book 16, chapter 21. She knows herself when, placed in mind among sinners, she remembers that she was made in the image of her Author and walks according to the order of the likeness received; but if she does not know it, she goes out from the secret of the heart into outward desires, and, led to the broad way, follows the examples of the peoples. The Lord, rebuking the fearful Church, reminds her of the grace given her against the snares of enemies. Your kids. Because they are trained not according to the rule of my commandments, but according to your errors. Beside, in the footsteps of the shepherds you will be last, not among the sheep but the kids. Or beside, that is, that you may be like the true shepherds, because hypocrites seem to follow good men.
1.8: 1.8 To the cavalry. As I freed the former people from Egyptian slavery, so I will free you from the hands of the persecutors, crushing Pharaoh, if you recognize yourself as my bride, freeing you from the slavery of the devil in the font of baptism reddened by the passion, the author of sin being drowned there. To my cavalry. Because the Lord does not wish the Church to be ignorant of herself, but diligently to attend to what gifts she has received and what she must suffer, after the threat he consequently coaxes her, as if he said: If you wish to understand how you ought to know yourself, understand to whom I have compared you, and then you will know yourself to be such through my benefits conferred on you, so that you ought not to be troubled. To the cavalry. The horseman is the bridegroom, as the prophet says: And his salvation is a riding (Habakkuk 3). As much then as my cavalry differs from the horses of Pharaoh, so much better are you than all other daughters. As that people was terrified by the chariots of Pharaoh coming upon them, but was saved by heavenly protection, and, the enemies drowned through the waters, was brought into the promised land, so the wave of death, which will meet all mortals, snatches the wicked to destruction and opens to the pious the way to salvation, and all the rest, which was fulfilled there bodily, is fulfilled here spiritually. He kindly rebukes the one who doubts, and lest she despair he strengthens her manfully in the faithful love that follows, where he compares her to Pharaoh's chariots. In the chariots of Pharaoh. That is, in the time of the chariots. And note the pride: Pharaoh is interpreted as crushing or scattering. Nor is it necessary that you begin to wander, since you have me as consoler, and prelates on whom you may lean, through whom you may stand firm.
